speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether deferring public transport fare increments to future years remains sustainable, given the anticipated continued rise in cost of living in Singapore; (b) whether the Ministry has mandated any measures to be taken by public transport operators to streamline processes and reduce expenses in order to mitigate rising costs; and (c) if so, what are these measures.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The fare formula reflects the general cost drivers of providing public transport services, based on macroeconomic factors such as core inflation, national wage growth and energy prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It provides for fares to be adjusted in tandem with changes in these cost drivers, rather than changes in operators' actual costs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In this way, the operators cannot assume that their cost increases will be matched by correspondingly higher fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Hence, they need to be disciplined in managing their costs and improving their productivity over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In setting fares, the PTC does not focus on the actual salaries paid by the operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The formula is based on the national wage index.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This allows operators to keep public transport sector salaries competitive with the rest of the economy, so that they are able to attract and retain their workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Wage increases that exceed changes in the national wage index will not be covered by the fare formula.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the past five years, the wages of public transport workers grew at a similar pace as the national wage index.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The fare formula also includes a Productivity Contribution, which reduces the allowable fare adjustment by 0.1 percentage points every year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This further incentivises the operators to look for continuous productivity improvements to reduce their costs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, the operators have been using joint tenders to achieve economies of scale, automating their maintenance processes and upskilling their workers to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The fare formula therefore avoids operators' costs from being directly passed on to commuters, while allowing commuters to benefit from productivity savings from the operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Guided by the formula, the PTC exercises judgement on how much of the allowable fare adjustment to implement each year, taking into consideration economic and social factors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, the PTC looks at affordability as measured by the estimated proportion of household income spent on public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the lower-income, this proportion has fallen from 3.1% in 2013 to 2.4% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For average public transport users, the figure has also reduced from 2.2% in 2013 to 1.7% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The quantum of allowable fare adjustment that is not implemented in a particular year is deferred and carried forward to future years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the 2022 Fare Review Exercise (FRE), the PTC deferred 10.6% percentage points of the fare increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Adding the deferred quantum of 10.6% to the fare formula output, the maximum allowable fare increase for 2023 was 22.6%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To keep public transport fares affordable for commuters and understanding that Singaporean families are currently facing higher costs of living, the PTC again decided not to grant the full quantum this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The remaining 15.6 percentage points will be deferred to future years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This amount is on top of the $2 billion annual subsidies to fund bus and train services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, the cost of public transport infrastructure is also fully funded by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Chua asked whether the PTC plans to "expunge" the 15.6 percentage points.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Don Wee asked if the PTC can "impose a moratorium" on future fare increases.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Please allow me to explain why their proposals are not sound, as these will affect the longer-term reliability and financial sustainability of our public transport system, to the detriment of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I had earlier mentioned that the fare formula reflects real cost increases in our economy, such as energy costs and wages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If the deferred fare amount is "expunged" as Mr Louis Chua proposed, or if fares are frozen for future years as Mr Don Wee suggested, it does not mean that these costs of running the public transport system will simply disappear into thin air.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Hence, I would like to ask Mr Chua and Mr Wee to clarify whether they are proposing for the operators to absorb this cost, or for taxpayers to bear a larger cost burden to provide higher Government subsidies on a permanent basis?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If it is the latter, they should elaborate how such a move will be funded every year and whether they are proposing for Singaporeans to pay additional taxes to do so?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I hope that is not what they have in mind.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If it is to ask the public transport operators to absorb the costs, we need to consider how this will impact their financial sustainability over time and in turn, affect their ability to provide accessible and reliable public transport services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Louis Chua asked about the profits of the public transport operators and Mr Don Wee suggested that we could freeze fares given that operators have been profitable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For buses, Government collects the fare revenue and pays the operators a service fee that is derived from competitive bids via bus contracting tenders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Overall, bus services are operating at a loss and that is why Government needs to provide about $1 billion in subsidies for buses every year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Expunging the deferred fare or freezing future fare increases will result in larger losses and higher Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For rail services, the operators collect the fares to cover their operating costs, so fares do impact the rail operators' profitability directly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We should not pretend that the deferred fare increases can somehow be expunged and magically disappear, or assume that future fare increases can be frozen without consequences to our public transport system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Making such populist moves will further enlarge the funding gap over time which must be supported by higher Government subsidies funded by taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not the responsible thing to do.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We need to be clear that Government subsidies are ultimately borne by current and future generations of taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The PTC will continue to ensure that fare adjustments each year are affordable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In each future FRE, the PTC will assess the cost increases as reflected by the fare formula, the deferred fare amount from previous years, as well as the impact on affordability for commuters, before deciding on the fare increase to be granted for that year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And when the opportunity arises, the PTC will consider whether it is possible to lower the total deferred fare amount so the gap will gradually reduce over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The PTC and Government are also mindful that fare increases affect different groups of commuters differently.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While it is important that commuters bear their fair share of cost increases, we are committed to ensuring that fares remain affordable, especially for concession groups such as seniors, students, lower-wage workers and Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These groups enjoy discounts of up to 70% off adult per-journey fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Within each concession group, there is a wide range of spending on public transport, depending on different commuting patterns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Among all seniors, persons with disabilities (PwDs) and individuals on the Workfare Transport Concession Scheme (WTCS), the median monthly spending on public transport is about $16, $24 and $35 respectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is expected to benefit about 60,000 commuters, including about 1,600 WTCS cardholders who currently pay per-journey fares and spend more than the monthly pass price of $96.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Concession cardholders who make fewer public transport journeys will continue to enjoy substantial discounts off adult per-journey fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When fares increase, the PTC requires rail operators to contribute a proportion of their increased fare revenue to the Public Transport Fund.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the coming year, the rail operators will contribute a total of $16 million.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Together with Government's contributions to the Fund, these monies are used to provide Public Transport Vouchers (PTVs) to help cushion the impact on lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the past decade, we have steadily enhanced the quality of our public transport system by expanding the network, and improving accessibility and reliability of services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These outcomes have been achieved through our strong tripartite partnership between the Government, operators and workers, while keeping fares affordable and the public transport system financially sustainable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the PTC take into consideration the recent number of train breakdowns before allowing for the increase in fares?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if so, will maintenance of service reliability be taken into account before we ask commuters to pay more?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, can the Ministry share and elaborate on some of the initiatives their transport operators are undertaking to reduce expenses that will not affect the reliability of our transport services?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For rail, the measurement that we use is what they call the "mean kilometres between failures" (MKBF).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Under the Bus Contracting Model, frequency of all basic bus services, by which I mean trunk services, are 15 minutes or less during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Feeder services run even more frequently at no more than eight minutes during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) will track the commuter demand and ensure that there is sufficient capacity by adjusting the frequencies where needed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And as I explained in this House previously, whenever there are new Build-To-Order developments, new demand, we will also look at whether we need to introduce new feeder services to serve these new estates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the fare formula, I explained that we have a productivity contribution component to incentivise them to do so, but on the ground, the operators have been working very closely with their suppliers, and also with the unions, with the help from our unions, together with the workers, to encourage a lot of ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In SMRT, for example, they focus a lot on "kaizen".

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They use this as a movement within the organisation to identify areas for improvement, to improve safety, to improve reliability and to also reduce costs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And these savings will help not only to keep our public transport system financially sustainable and avoid subsidies going up and up over the years, importantly, I think that it is also in the spirit of continuous improvement and we empower the workers to look for ways in which they can make things better, improve the processes and the ground-up initiatives are then given top-down support by management.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is in relation to the PTC's work, I understand that it is guided by the fare formula.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But if you look at the increase that is been granted, 7%, I think that is well above what we are seeing in the overall inflation rates here in Singapore, so far.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If you look at the 15.6 percentage-point increase that is going to be deferred to the future, this is going to cause a significant effect, a lasting effect into the increases in public transport fares for Singaporeans, given that this could have a snowballing effect, since there will be the deferred increase and future increases to consider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in that sense, would the Minister not consider, even if not expunging, then moderating the level of increase, just as it did in the fare review exercise in 2021, when the PTC did not fully agree with the outputs from the fare formula?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in terms of financial sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In relation to the written answer which Minister has partially responded to, when I look at the public transport operator, should we not look at the public transport system as a whole, and in that sense, would the Minister not agree that if we look at the returns that some of these operators are generating – one of them, for example, is actually generating close to 11% return on equity in the last one year and 13% in the last five years – one would struggle to see how the financial sustainability of the operator, at this point in time, is actually in question?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And yes, that is part of the fare formula.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, we also need to look at other components that affect the cost of the operators, but taken, as I explained my main reply, not their actual cost but as a benchmark looking at the national wage index and looking at the energy index, because these are significant cost components that will affect overall public transport operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is why the fare formula, using these components, we worked it out last year, we carried it forward, 10.6%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you add that to the 10.6%, the total is 22.6%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But this is where – perhaps Mr Chua and myself, we may not disagree so much – that the PTC does not just go for the formula maximum amount and say, "It is 22.6%, therefore I go for 22.6%".

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I explained, they will exercise judgement, they will consider the impact on commuters, on affordability and then after that, they will exercise judgement in terms of what is the level to set and how much to defer.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why I explained earlier that if we do not find ways, in subsequent years when we can, to gradually to reduce this gap, and if we expunge it, what it means is that the $300 million will remain as a permanent subsidy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And it will add on to the existing subsidies that we already provide: $1 billion for rail, $1 billion for bus.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think it is a valid point that we do want to look at affordability on commuters, we do want to consider the impact, including on the overall cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And that is why the PTC exercises judgement and it is not just driven by the formula.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I have explained this in my main reply as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We need to look at bus and rail separately.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For buses, the fares that are being collected do not go to the operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The fares that are being collected actually do not go to the revenue of the bus operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The revenue of the bus operations come from LTA, when we tender out bus contracts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, hopefully, over time, it will allow us to squeeze out more productivity gains, more savings, that we can then pass on to taxpayers and to commuters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I fully empathise with the delicate balance that has to be struck.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My supplementary question relates to whether the Minister would consider additional tiers within the hybrid cards and calibrating across these tiers to better reflect the diversity in usage patterns.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even on the concession cards, I believe that the discounts given to seniors also reflects the very different usage patterns, using the buses and off-peak hours, which do not drive as much of the cost of the transportation network.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, as our seniors become a larger and larger share, and will eventually become 25% of our population, would the Minister agree that there may be room to consider a slightly more differentiated approach to our hybrid cards for seniors, to allow more people to benefit?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The figures that the Minister cited $16, $24, are quite far from the hybrid card costs of $58 today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, could we allow a bigger diversity of seniors to benefit from the subsidies?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not an overall increase, but a better calibration across different tiers, where you have your young seniors who may still be working, you have your Pioneer Generation – these groups have very different usage patterns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why in this year's FRE, the PTC has looked at how to lower the cost of the concession pass for the different vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, we subsidise public transport services by more than $2 billion every year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you were to translate it to per journey, it is more than $1 per journey.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, for the concession card holders, they enjoy discounts of up to 70% of the adult per journey fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is even if you do not buy the concession pass, because we do have a separate rate for the different concession groups.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And the benefit applies to all concession users, whether they are light users, moderate users or heavy users.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I understand Ms Mariam Jaafar's point, that because today, the concession passes are set to cater to people who are heavy users – if I understood her correctly, I think she is asking whether we can have different tiers of passes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I just want to raise one factual point, that I hope Ms Mariam agrees with me, which is that it is quite difficult to tell ex ante when a person walks in and say, "I want to buy a concession pass", whether this person is a light, moderate or heavy user.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We cannot tell – ex post, you can tell, but not ex ante.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when this person comes in and wants to buy a concession pass, unless we set a limit to how many times this person can use the pass, which then goes against our current concession pass concept – which is once you buy the concession pass, it is unlimited, it is like a buffet, you can use as many times as you like.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think we can take a look, but I do not think we can implement the current all-you-can-use approach and have different tiers because it is not possible to tell ex ante whether the person is a light, moderate or heavy user.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even for workers and the WTCS, the PTV covers less than half a month's public transport expenses per worker.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, many families have multiple family members working or schooling, and each of them may need help to cover the cost of public transport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the PTVs be provided on an individual basis rather than per household to help larger families that are working hard to make ends meet?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, one of commuters' bugbears is that despite increases in bus fares, bus routes – especially trunk services which are popular among the elderly – continue to be rationalised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While this boosts operator profits and Government savings, it diminishes service quality for the affected commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even to this day, my residents in Bedok Reservoir still complain to me about reduced bus services and request for the return of bus services 66 and 506.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will LTA continue to rationalise bus services despite this increase in bus fares?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, the public transport fare hikes coincide with record-high COE prices and increases in fares and fees for taxis and private hire vehicles in July.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans cannot help but feel squeezed no matter which mode of transport they take.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Did the PTC consider the recent increases in private transport costs when approving the public transport fare hike and its impact on Singapore's plans to become a car-lite city?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That said, I do agree with Mr Giam that families and households have different compositions – some have more members.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The way we have done it, Sir, is as with past exercises, households with genuine needs but may have missed the eligibility criteria or if they need more help because they have a larger family size, they can appeal to their local community centres.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The appeals will then be considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has to be very carefully considered because there are commuters who are affected.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We try our best not to do that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But because there are new estates that are coming up, including, I am sure, in Mr Giam's constituency, we do need to also cater new feeder services to meet new demand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we do not find a way to re-allocate some of the resources from existing services to meet new demand, then the concern there is that the bill will keep growing for commuters and for taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when we have to take away some of these longer trunk routes, the considerations are, first, is there an alternative?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we do not take away if there is no alternative.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, is there a parallel Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) route or line that the commuter can take?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The concept that I hope Mr Giam can help us as well to explain to his residents, is that we encourage people to take public transport as much as possible within the town, feeder services to bring them from their homes or near their homes to the key transport notes like bus interchanges and MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And then for the longer trunk routes, gradually as we develop our MRT system and it becomes better connected, a more efficient way is to use the MRT to cater to the demand for the longer trunk routes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, think about it as feeder services mainly for the local, bringing you to key transport nodes; and then the MRT to cater to longer trunk routes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think if we can help to move towards such a system, it will be more efficient and also from a connectivity point of view, better for commuters.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Acting Minister if there is further upside to increase ridership?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whether with increased ridership, you can improve the overall financials of the operators running the public transport and hence, help to reduce further fare increases?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, our target is to further increase the public transport modal share.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not only because it will help with the cost recovery ratio or the financial sustainability of the public transport system – I mean, that is one benefit as Mr Liang highlighted – but also from the environmental sustainability point of view, because public transport is more environmentally sustainable than private cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Certainly, I think that is a direction that we want to encourage Singapore to head towards.
